planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring or fall; Clouds of Perfume blooms in mid-spring and is best sited where its strong fragrance can be enjoyed at close range, such as along a shaded path or near a seating area.

directions: Plant divisions or potted starts in part shade to full shade in moist, humus-rich soil in spring or fall, spacing plants about a foot apart so the spreading mats knit together within a season or two. Clouds of Perfume is prized above other woodland phlox selections for its unusually strong, sweet fragrance, carried on airy clusters of pale blue-lavender flowers held just above the foliage in mid-spring. Like other forms of Phlox divaricata, it spreads gently by trailing stems that root as they go, forming a loose semi-evergreen groundcover that fills in shaded beds without becoming aggressive. Divide congested clumps every three to four years and keep soil evenly moist through the spring growth period to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Phlox divaricata and P. pilosa Trial Garden Report

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall; give afternoon shade in warmer zones and consistent moisture during the spring bloom and growth period.

directions: Plant divisions in part shade in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in spring or fall, allowing plants to spread naturally into a loose groundcover over two to three seasons. Selected from wild Texas populations by plantsman Don Jacobs of Eco Gardens, this cultivar produces notably larger flowers in a deep purple-violet shade that stands out among the paler blues and lavenders typical of the species. It shares the same woodland habit as other forms of wild blue phlox, forming semi-evergreen mats that spread by rooting stems and blooming heavily for several weeks in mid-spring before deciduous tree canopies fully leaf out. Provide light afternoon shade in warmer zones and steady moisture during the spring growth period to keep the foliage from stressing in summer heat.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Phlox divaricata and P. pilosa Trial Garden Report
